mechanism.title: The first five minutes, step by step
steps: Restate the problem in one sentence to confirm scope: “A service where riders request autos and nearby drivers accept, in one country, mobile apps only.”
Functional requirements: list 3–5 core user actions and agree which are in scope (request ride, match driver, track trip, pay) and which are out (ratings, scheduled rides, chat).
Non-functional requirements: ask for scale (daily active users, peak factor), latency targets, availability, consistency needs per feature, durability, and regional or regulatory constraints.
Write explicit assumptions where the interviewer has no preference: “10 million DAU, peak 3× average, 99.9% availability, match within 5 seconds at p99.”
Turn assumptions into anchor numbers you will reuse: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth. Do the arithmetic aloud and round sensibly.
Confirm priorities: “I’ll focus on matching and location updates, and treat payments as a black box unless you want me to go there.”

useWhen: Always, in the first few minutes, before drawing any boxes.
Again whenever the interviewer adds a twist ('now make it work offline'): restate the changed requirement before redesigning.
avoidWhen: Do not spend more than about 5 minutes of a 45-minute interview on requirements; move on with stated assumptions.
Do not ask questions you will not use; every number you gather should change a design decision.

rows: How many daily users? Peak factor?
How fast must a match feel?
Can two drivers accept one ride?
Conditional writes or locks on the ride

numbers.title: Turning assumptions into anchor numbers
assumptions: 10 million DAU; each user makes 2 ride requests per day
steps: Average per second = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231.
Peak per second = 231 × 3 = 693, call it about 700.
Driver location pings: 500,000 online drivers every 4 seconds gives 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 writes per second, far larger than ride requests, so location ingestion is the scaling hot spot.
numbers.result: Anchor numbers show that location pings, not ride requests, dominate load, which tells you where to spend the deep dive.

india.title: Clarifying a “design an IRCTC-like booking system” prompt
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: If asked to design a train-booking system for India, strong candidates first separate normal booking from the Tatkal window, when demand spikes sharply at the opening minute. They ask whether the focus is search, seat inventory or payments, whether waitlist and RAC (reservation against cancellation) rules are in scope, and what consistency is required: a berth must never be sold twice, so seat allocation is strongly consistent while availability displays can be slightly stale. Stating “I’ll assume a burst of a few lakh booking attempts in the first minute, an illustrative estimate” lets them size queues and inventory locks instead of guessing later.

pitfalls.trap: Jumping straight to drawing a load balancer and a database.
pitfalls.say: “Before designing, let me confirm the core features and the scale, so I size the right parts.”

pitfalls.trap: Collecting numbers and never using them.
pitfalls.say: “At about 700 peak ride requests per second but 125,000 location writes per second, I’ll focus the design on location ingestion.”

takeaways: Clarify scope before drawing anything.
Ask only questions that change design decisions.
Write assumptions down and turn them into anchor numbers.
Use the numbers to choose where to deep-dive.

extraQuestions.prompt: 10 million DAU each make 2 requests a day with a 3× peak factor. What is the approximate peak request rate?

choices.label: About 700 per second
About 230 per second
About 20,000 per second
About 70 per second

extraQuestions.explanation: 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second on average; × 3 ≈ 693 at peak.

115.diagram:
restate -> functional (in/out) -> non-functional (scale, latency, consistency, availability)
 -> assumptions -> anchor numbers -> agreed focus

mechanism.title: Running a deep dive
steps: Pick the component where the requirements are hardest: the hot path at peak, the strongest consistency need, or the biggest data volume. Say why you picked it.
State the problem precisely: “Two drivers can accept the same ride within milliseconds; we must allow exactly one.”
Offer two or three options, each in one sentence.
Compare with the trade-off template: “Option A gives X at the cost of Y; option B gives Y but costs Z. Given our requirement W, I choose A.”
Go one level deeper on the chosen option: data model, the exact query or write, failure cases, and the numbers it must handle.
Close the loop: name what would make you switch options later (for example, 'if accepts exceed 10,000 per second on one city partition, I'd split by zone').

useWhen: Whenever you choose a technology or pattern, and whenever the interviewer asks “why not X?”.
On the one or two components that carry the most risk; depth beats breadth.
avoidWhen: Do not deep-dive into something generic, like the load balancer algorithm, while the hard problem (matching, consistency) stays vague.
Do not use absolutes such as “always use Kafka” or “NoSQL is faster”; tie every claim to a requirement.

rows: “X fits because we need …; the cost is …”
“It scales to about N per second per node; we need M, so about M ÷ N nodes”
“Cache menus for 5 minutes, invalidate on edit; prices at checkout from the database”
“Strong for ride acceptance, eventual for driver locations shown on the map”

numbers.title: Comparing two options with numbers
assumptions: Ride accept rate at peak 700 per second across a city
Option A: conditional update on the ride row in PostgreSQL, about 2 ms each
Option B: a Redis lock per ride, about 0.5 ms each plus lock expiry handling
steps: Option A load: 700 writes per second, each touching one row, which one PostgreSQL primary handles comfortably.
Total busy time for option A = 700 × 2 ms = 1,400 ms of work per second, spread over many connections and cores.
Option B is faster per call but adds a second system whose failover can drop locks, plus a lease to manage.
Since option A meets the load with the source of truth, choose A and mention B only if accepts grow 10× or more.
numbers.result: Use numbers to show the simpler option is enough, and name the threshold at which you would switch.

india.title: Deep dive on Tatkal seat allocation
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: In a train-booking interview, the right deep dive is seat allocation during the Tatkal opening, not the search page. A good answer compares a queue in front of the inventory service (fair and smooth, but adds waiting time), conditional decrements per train-class-date row (simple and strongly consistent, but one hot row per popular train), and pre-splitting a train’s quota into several counters (more parallelism, slightly more complex rebalancing). The candidate then picks, for example, a queue plus conditional decrements, explains the failure cases (payment fails, hold expires and the seat returns), and states the illustrative load the design must take.

pitfalls.say: “For ride acceptance we need a conditional write on one row; PostgreSQL does that at 700 per second easily, so I’d keep it there.”
“The hard part here is double acceptance, so I’ll go deep on that rather than load-balancer algorithms.”

takeaways: Deep-dive where the requirements are hardest.
Use “X gives A at the cost of B; given W, I choose X”.
Replace absolutes with numbers and requirements.
Say what would make you change your mind.

extraQuestions.prompt: Which statement best follows the trade-off template?

choices.label: “A conditional update in PostgreSQL costs a hot row; at 700/s that is fine, so I choose it”
“PostgreSQL is the best database, so I always pick it for every system I design”
“Redis scales infinitely, so I put everything in Redis and skip the database”
“We should always use microservices, because they scale better than monoliths”

extraQuestions.explanation: It names the cost (a hot row), puts a number on the load, and then decides. The others are absolutes with no cost: no database is best for every system, Redis does not scale without limit and is a weak sole system of record, and microservices bring network and operational costs of their own.

116.diagram: pick hardest part -> state problem -> 2-3 options -> trade-off template -> deeper on choice -> 'switch if ...'

mechanism.title: How common mistakes unfold, and how to catch them
steps: No scope: the candidate starts drawing before agreeing on features and scale, then designs the wrong thing for 20 minutes.
Over-engineering: Kafka, microservices, multi-region active-active and a service mesh for a system with 50 requests per second.
Unused numbers: the estimate says 2 TB per year, then the design ignores it (or contradicts it by sharding across 100 nodes).
Silence: long stretches of thinking without speaking, so the interviewer cannot follow or help.
Ignoring hints: the interviewer asks “what if two users book the same seat?” and the candidate moves on.

Recovery: when you notice any of these, say so plainly ('I over-built this; at 50 requests per second one service and PostgreSQL are enough'), simplify and continue. Correcting yourself is a positive signal.

useWhen: Use this list as a self-check every ten minutes: scope agreed? numbers used? speaking aloud? following hints?
Use the recovery script whenever you realise you are off track.
avoidWhen: Do not hide a mistake and hope the interviewer misses it; they almost never do.
Do not overcorrect into designing nothing; keep a working end-to-end design on the board.

rows: Restate and agree core features first
Tie each component to a number
Narrate the options you are weighing
Treat a repeated question as the priority

numbers.title: Is Kafka justified here?
assumptions: Internal tool: 5,000 users, each creating 20 events per day
Kafka cluster minimum: 3 brokers, plus operations effort
steps: Events per day = 5,000 × 20 = 100,000.
Average per second = 100,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1.2.
Even at a 10× peak that is about 12 events per second, which a PostgreSQL table or a simple managed queue handles easily.
A three-broker Kafka cluster adds cost and on-call load for no benefit at this scale.
numbers.result: About 1 event per second does not need Kafka; matching tools to numbers is the cure for over-engineering.

india.title: Over-building a college fest ticketing app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A candidate asked to design ticketing for a college fest in Kolkata, about 20,000 tickets sold over two weeks, proposes Kubernetes, Kafka, Cassandra and multi-region failover. The interviewer asks for the numbers: 20,000 tickets over 14 days is about 1,430 a day, and even if a quarter sell in the first hour, that is about 5,000 in an hour, around 1.4 per second. The strong recovery is: “I over-built this. A single web app with PostgreSQL, a unique constraint on seat ids, a payment gateway webhook and a CDN for the poster is enough; I’d add a queue only if launch traffic proves bursty.”

pitfalls.trap: Defending an over-built design when challenged.
pitfalls.say: “You’re right, at about 1.4 tickets per second this is over-built; let me simplify to one service and PostgreSQL.”

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring a repeated question from the interviewer.
pitfalls.say: “You’ve asked about double booking twice, so let me address it now: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) makes the second booking fail cleanly.”
“I’m weighing a queue against direct writes; the queue smooths bursts but adds latency. Given our numbers, direct writes are fine.”

takeaways: Agree scope before designing.
Match every component to a number.
Think aloud; silence hides good reasoning.
Recover openly; self-correction is a strength.

extraQuestions.prompt: A system handles about 1–12 events per second. A candidate proposes a three-broker Kafka cluster. What is the best feedback?

choices.label: Overkill: a table or managed queue is enough
Kafka is needed for any event-driven design
Use five brokers instead, to leave room to grow
Fine, because Kafka is popular and widely known

extraQuestions.explanation: At 1–12 events a second, a database table polled by a worker, or a managed queue, is plenty, while a three-broker cluster adds brokers to run, monitor and upgrade. Nothing ties events to Kafka, more brokers make it worse, and popularity is not a requirement. Have the follow-up ready: switch when the rate reaches thousands a second, or when many consumers need to replay history.

117.diagram:
every ~10 min: scope agreed? -> numbers used? -> talking aloud? -> hints followed?
 off track -> name it -> simplify -> continue

mechanism.title: A communication rhythm for a 45-minute design interview
steps: Minutes 0–5: requirements and assumptions, spoken and written down.
Minutes 5–10: estimates, said out loud with the assumptions behind them.
Minutes 10–15: the API: key endpoints with request and response shapes.
Minutes 15–25: a simple end-to-end design that works for the core flow, narrating each box: what it does and why it exists.

Minutes 25–40: deep dive and evolution: add caching, sharding, queues or replicas one at a time, each tied to a number, and cover failure modes; check in with the interviewer about which area to go deep on.
Minutes 40–45: summarise the design, the main trade-offs, what you would monitor and what you would do next with more time.

useWhen: Narrate continuously: options, the choice, and the reason.
Collaborate: ask “shall I go deeper on matching or on payments?” at natural checkpoints, and use the interviewer’s hints.
avoidWhen: Do not monologue for 15 minutes without checking in.
Do not present a final complex design in one go; evolve from simple to scaled so each addition is justified.

rows: Restates the problem, asks scoped questions
Simple first, then scaled step by step

numbers.title: Budgeting the 45 minutes
assumptions: The same six-stage plan used in Lesson 1, the Interview Playbook and Interview mode: 5, 5, 5, 10, 15, 5 minutes
steps: Requirements: 5 minutes, about 11% of 45.
Estimates and API: 5 + 5 = 10 minutes.
Simple design: 10 minutes; deep dive and failures: 15 minutes.
numbers.result: The deep dive gets the largest single block, 15 minutes; protect it by keeping requirements to about 5. If you reach minute 25 without a complete request path on the board, say so and simplify.

india.title: A food-delivery design interview, narrated
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Asked to design a Zomato- or Swiggy-style ordering flow, a strong candidate says: “I’ll start with one order service and PostgreSQL so the core flow works: browse menu, place order, pay, track. At about 1,000 orders per second at dinner peak, an illustrative estimate, PostgreSQL handles writes, so first I’ll cache menus, since they are read about a hundred times per order. Shall I go deeper on rider assignment or on payment consistency?” The interviewer picks rider assignment, and the candidate evolves the design there, keeping the rest simple. Each step is spoken, justified and checked.

pitfalls.say: “I’m adding a cache in front of menus because they’re read about a hundred times per order and change rarely.”

pitfalls.trap: Running out of time before failures and a summary.
pitfalls.say: “We have about eight minutes left, so let me cover what breaks and how we detect it, then summarise the trade-offs.”

pitfalls.trap: Using jargon without explaining the choice.
pitfalls.say: “I’ll use an outbox here, which means the order and its event commit in one transaction, so no event is lost if we crash.”
“Good point about duplicate payments; I’ll add an idempotency key on the payment request.”

takeaways: Think aloud: options, choice, reason.
Check in at natural points and use hints.
Start simple, then evolve under the numbers.
Keep time for failures and a summary.

extraQuestions.prompt: Why present a simple working design before adding caches, shards and queues?

choices.label: Each addition can then be justified by a requirement or number
Interviewers prefer small diagrams that fit on one screen
Complex designs are always wrong in an interview setting
It avoids having to discuss any trade-offs at all

extraQuestions.explanation: Evolving step by step shows why each component exists rather than presenting an unexplained final picture.

118.diagram: 0-5 reqs | 5-10 estimates | 10-15 API | 15-25 simple design | 25-40 deep dive + failures | 40-45 summary

mechanism.title: Estimating with the cheat sheet, step by step
steps: Memorise rough latency orders: L1 cache about 1 ns; main memory about 100 ns; SSD random read about 100 µs; same-zone network round trip about 0.5 ms; disk seek about 10 ms; cross-continent round trip about 150 ms. These are order-of-magnitude figures, not exact.
Memorise powers of two and ten: 2 to the power 10 ≈ 1 thousand, 2 to the power 20 ≈ 1 million, 2 to the power 30 ≈ 1 billion, 2 to the power 40 ≈ 1 trillion.
Memorise the day: 86,400 seconds, so 1 million requests per day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion per day is about 11,600 per second.
Estimate requests per second: daily actions ÷ 86,400, then multiply by a peak factor (2–5×).
Estimate storage: items per day × bytes per item × retention days × replication factor.
Estimate servers: peak requests per second ÷ requests one server handles (measure or assume, for example 1,000–5,000 simple requests per second), plus headroom for failures.

useWhen: Any time a design choice depends on scale: caching, sharding, number of servers, bandwidth, storage tier.
Sanity checks: if an estimate says one server handles everything, do not shard; if it says petabytes, do not use one database.
avoidWhen: Do not chase precision; one significant figure is enough.
Do not quote latency figures as exact facts about specific hardware; say “roughly” and use them for orders of magnitude.

numbers.title: Sizing photo storage for a social app
assumptions: Average 500 KB after compression; keep 3 sizes adding 50% more
Replication or erasure-coding overhead 1.5×; keep 5 years
steps: Bytes per photo with sizes = 500 KB × 1.5 = 750 KB.
Per day = 5,000,000 × 750 KB = 3,750,000,000 KB, which is about 3.75 TB.
Per year = 3.75 TB × 365 ≈ 1,369 TB, about 1.4 PB.
Five years with 1.5× storage overhead = 1.4 PB × 5 × 1.5 ≈ 10.5 PB, which points to object storage rather than any database.
numbers.result: About 10 PB over five years: the estimate itself decides the storage tier.

india.title: Latency from Indian users to servers
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A user in Chennai calling an API hosted in a US region pays a round trip of roughly 200–250 ms before any server work, and a page needing four sequential calls pays that four times, about a second. Hosting in an Indian cloud region (Mumbai, Hyderabad or Chennai offerings exist from major providers) cuts round trips to tens of milliseconds for most Indian users. That is why Indian consumer apps keep latency-sensitive APIs in India and push static assets to CDN edges in many Indian cities. These latency numbers are typical orders of magnitude, not measurements of a specific network.

pitfalls.say: “Roughly 20 million a day is about 230 per second; with 3× peak, about 700.”

pitfalls.trap: Never using the cheat sheet in decisions.
pitfalls.say: “A same-zone round trip is about 0.5 ms, so five sequential service calls add only a few milliseconds; cross-region calls would add hundreds.”

takeaways: Know latency orders of magnitude from nanoseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.
Divide daily counts by 86,400, then apply a peak factor.
Storage = items × size × retention × replication.
Round to one significant figure and let the result pick the architecture.

extraQuestions.prompt: About how many requests per second is 1 billion requests per day on average?

choices.label: About 11,600
About 1,160
About 116,000
About 86,400

extraQuestions.explanation: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,574, roughly 11,600 per second before any peak factor.

119.diagram:
ns: L1 (1) -> RAM (100)
µs: SSD read (100)
ms: zone RTT (0.5) -> disk seek (10) -> India-US RTT (~200+)
 day = 86,400 s | 1M/day ≈ 12/s | 1B/day ≈ 11,600/s

mechanism.title: Mapping a requirement to a pattern
steps: Read-heavy (reads much greater than writes): cache-aside with Redis, a CDN for static and cacheable responses, read replicas, and denormalised read models.
Write-heavy (high ingest): append-only logs (Kafka), LSM-based stores (Cassandra), batching, partitioning by a high-cardinality key, and asynchronous processing.
Real-time updates to clients: WebSockets or server-sent events for push, pub/sub to fan out, presence in memory with TTLs.
Correctness under concurrency (money, inventory, bookings): ACID transactions, conditional writes, unique constraints, idempotency keys, outbox for events, sagas across services.
Search and location: inverted index (Elasticsearch) for text, geohash or H3 cells for nearby queries, kept in sync from the source of truth by CDC.
Analytics: CDC into a warehouse or lake with columnar storage; stream processing for second-level dashboards.

useWhen: Use the map to propose a first design quickly once requirements are clear.
Combine patterns per feature: one product can be read-heavy in the catalogue and correctness-critical at checkout.
avoidWhen: Do not apply a pattern just because the system “sounds like” one category; check the numbers.
Do not use one pattern for every feature; the cache that helps the catalogue would harm the wallet balance.

numbers.title: Classifying a feature by its numbers
assumptions: Product page: 50,000 reads per second, 50 writes per second
Rider location: 125,000 writes per second, 10,000 reads per second
steps: Product page read-to-write ratio = 50,000 ÷ 50 = 1,000 to 1, so it is read-heavy: cache plus CDN.
Rider location write-to-read ratio = 125,000 ÷ 10,000 = 12.5 to 1, so it is write-heavy: in-memory geo store, partitioned by city, with short TTLs.
The two features in the same app need opposite patterns.
Checkout, at a few hundred writes per second, is correctness-first: transactions and idempotency keys rather than caches.
numbers.result: Ratios, not product names, decide patterns: 1,000 to 1 reads means cache; 12.5 to 1 writes means an ingest-optimised store.

india.title: One quick-commerce app, four patterns
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A 10-minute grocery app in India shows all four families at once. The catalogue is read-heavy, served from a cache and CDN images. Rider and order-tracking updates are real-time, pushed to the customer’s phone over a persistent connection. Stock reservation at each dark store is correctness-critical, using conditional decrements and idempotent order creation so that the last packet of milk is not sold twice. Product search uses an inverted index with Hinglish synonyms, filtered by the customer’s nearest dark store using geo cells. Naming the requirement first, then the pattern, then the component, is what interviewers want to hear.

pitfalls.say: “The catalogue is read-heavy, so it’s cached; stock reservation must be exact, so it goes to the database with a conditional write.”

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting that one product mixes patterns.
pitfalls.say: “The same app is read-heavy in the catalogue and correctness-critical at checkout, so I design those two paths differently.”
“Because location updates are write-heavy at about 125,000 per second, I’d use a partitioned in-memory geo store rather than a relational table.”

takeaways: Name the requirement, then the pattern, then the component.
Read-to-write ratios decide caching versus ingest designs.
Different features of one product need different patterns.
Correctness-critical paths never rely on caches.

extraQuestions.prompt: A product page gets 50,000 reads/s and 50 writes/s. Which pattern fits first?

choices.label: Cache-aside plus CDN: reads are 1,000× writes
Kafka in front of every read request
Two-phase commit across the replicas
A write-optimised LSM store for the page

extraQuestions.explanation: A 1,000 to 1 read-to-write ratio is the classic case for caching.

120.diagram:
requirement -> pattern -> component
read-heavy -> cache/CDN -> Redis
write-heavy -> log/LSM -> Kafka/Cassandra
correctness -> txn/idempotency -> Postgres
real-time -> push -> WebSockets
search/geo -> index/cells -> Elasticsearch/H3
